title: Categories and indicators of abuse and neglect, including domestic abuse
blurb: Name the four categories of abuse, spot the NICE alerting features, and recognise children as victims of domestic abuse in their own right.
question: Ruby, 2, attends the emergency department with scalds to both feet in a sock-like pattern with a sharp upper line. Her father says she climbed into a hot bath herself. Which features raise concern, and what category of abuse is suspected?

teach.body: Working Together 2026 defines four categories of abuse: physical abuse, emotional abuse, sexual abuse and neglect. They often overlap, and 'some level of emotional abuse is involved in all types of maltreatment'. Abuse can happen in the family, in institutions, outside the home or wholly online, by adults or by other children. NICE CG89 lists the alerting features that should make you 'consider' or 'suspect' maltreatment.
teach.cite: Working Together 2026, Appendix A; NICE CG89

teach.caption: Sexual abuse is not committed by adult males alone: women and other children can abuse.

rows.label: Meaning
values: Serious level of concern, not proof

rows.label: Example
values: Bruise in the shape of a hand

Suspect maltreatment when...

Hand, grip, ligature or implement shape; ears, neck, buttocks; clusters

teach.caption: An 'unsuitable explanation' is implausible, inadequate or inconsistent, including with the child's development. A cultural explanation is also unsuitable.

teach.h: Neglect and emotional abuse: what you may see
items: Persistent infestations such as scabies or head lice (consider neglect).
Repeatedly missed essential appointments or prescribed treatment not given.
Untreated dental decay where treatment is available.
Persistently dirty and smelly, seen early in the day.
Marked change in behaviour, withdrawal, recurrent nightmares.
Over-friendliness to strangers or excessively 'good' behaviour to avoid disapproval.

teach.body: The Domestic Abuse Act 2021 s3 recognises a child who sees, hears or experiences the effects of domestic abuse, and is related to the victim or perpetrator, as a victim in their own right. The Children Act's definition of harm also includes impairment from seeing or hearing the ill-treatment of another. Under the statutory definition, abuse is between people aged 16 or over who are personally connected, so 16 and 17-year-olds can be victims of abuse in their own relationships.
teach.cite: Domestic Abuse Act 2021 ss1-3; Children Act 1989 s31(9)

teach.h: When a parent discloses domestic abuse

steps.label: Assess risk
steps.sub: To her and to the children

teach.body: Scalds to both feet in a stocking pattern with sharply delineated borders indicate forced immersion (CG89 1.1.6). A climbing accident does not account for this forced-immersion pattern, so the explanation is unsuitable. The nurse treats the burns, records the father's account verbatim with body maps, informs the safeguarding lead and refers to children's social care for suspected physical abuse.

teach.text: Neglect is persistent failure, not a single lapse, and it is not the same as poverty: NICE notes it can be hard to distinguish material poverty from neglect (CG89 1.3.4). But a family's choices about care do not excuse failure to meet needs. And do not wait for proof: 'suspect' already means refer.

items: Four categories: physical (including FII), emotional, sexual, neglect; they overlap.
Bruises shaped like a hand or implement, or on ears, neck or buttocks: suspect maltreatment.
Glove or stocking scalds with sharp borders, buttocks or perineum: forced immersion.
Neglect: persistent; includes missed essential care, untreated dental decay, poor supervision.
Children who see, hear or experience domestic abuse are victims in their own right (DA Act 2021 s3).
Consider = possible explanation; suspect = serious concern, refer.

summary: You can now classify abuse into the four Working Together categories and recognise NICE CG89 alerting features for each. You can also respond when domestic abuse is disclosed, treating the child as a victim in their own right.

A.q: A health visitor sees Kacper, 3. He has extensive untreated dental decay, has missed four hospital appointments and is often in dirty clothes. His parents can access treatment. Which category of abuse is most likely?
options: Emotional abuse
Neglect
Physical abuse
Fabricated or induced illness
A.why: Persistent failure to ensure access to medical and dental care and to meet basic needs is neglect (Working Together 2026; CG89 1.3).

whyNot.0: Emotional abuse may coexist, but the pattern described is failure to meet basic needs.
whyNot.3: FII involves fabricated or induced symptoms, not missed care.

A.q: On a children's ward, a mother repeatedly calls her 7-year-old son 'disgusting' and 'a baby' in front of others because he wets the bed. Which category does this most closely fit?
options: Neglect
Fabricated or induced illness
Emotional abuse
Sexual abuse
A.why: Persistently conveying to a child that he is worthless or inadequate is emotional abuse.

whyNot.0: Neglect is failure to meet needs; this is active belittling.
whyNot.1: No illness is being fabricated or induced.

A.q: Leo, 3, has several bruises. His father says he is 'always falling over'. Which distribution is most suggestive of maltreatment?
options: Bruises over both shins and both knees
A bruise on the forehead
Bruises on both elbows
Bruises on both ears and the neck
A.why: CG89 1.1.2: with an unsuitable explanation, bruises on non-bony parts such as the ears, or on the neck, should make you suspect maltreatment.

whyNot.0: Shins and knees are common sites of accidental bruising in toddlers.
whyNot.1: A forehead bruise over bone is common after a fall.
whyNot.2: Elbows are bony and often bruised in falls.

B.q: Finn, 6, is admitted with asthma. He tells the nurse he hides under his bed when his dad shouts at and hits his mum, and he has started wetting the bed. How should the nurse view Finn?
options: As a victim of domestic abuse in his own right
As a witness, with his mother as the victim
As a child in need, as he has no physical injuries
As a concern for adult services to manage
B.why: DA Act 2021 s3: a child who sees, hears or experiences the effects of domestic abuse, and is related to either party, is a victim in their own right.

whyNot.1: The law recognises Finn as a victim, not just a witness.
whyNot.2: Absence of injury does not limit the response; harm includes witnessing ill-treatment.
whyNot.3: Finn's safety is a children's safeguarding matter.

B.q: Ella, 9, says her 14-year-old cousin makes her touch him when he babysits. A colleague says this is 'experimentation between children'. What is the best response?
options: Agree, and advise the parents to improve supervision when babysitting
Refer it as child sexual abuse affecting both children
Wait for further disclosures before acting
Refer the cousin to the police as the offender
B.why: Sexual abuse can be committed by other children. A 14-year-old coercing a 9-year-old is abuse; both children need a safeguarding response.

whyNot.0: The age gap and coercion make this abuse, not experimentation.
whyNot.3: Ella needs protection through social care, not only a police report about the cousin.

B.q: Which burn pattern most strongly suggests a deliberate scald?
options: Splash marks on the chest and one arm
A scald on one forearm with irregular, spreading edges
Symmetrical scalds to both feet with sharp borders
A small contact burn on a fingertip
B.why: CG89 1.1.6: symmetrical, glove or stocking scalds with sharply delineated borders indicate forced immersion.

whyNot.0: Splash patterns fit accidental pulling of a hot drink.
whyNot.3: Small fingertip burns are typical of exploratory accidents.

C.q: During her child's eczema review, Mrs Begum quietly says her husband checks her phone, controls her money and last week pushed her down the stairs. Their children are 4 and 7. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Give her a leaflet and review at the next appointment
Speak to her husband to understand his view
Advise her to contact the police when she is ready
See her alone, assess risk and refer the children
C.why: Coercive control and violence create risk to her and to the children, who are victims in their own right. See her safely alone, assess risk and refer the children to social care.

whyNot.0: Delay leaves her and the children at risk.
whyNot.1: Confronting the perpetrator may escalate danger.
whyNot.2: The nurse must act on the children's safety now.

C.q: Lily, 5, has a vaginal discharge and swabs confirm gonorrhoea. Her mother is shocked and says Lily 'must have caught it from a towel'. What is the most appropriate action?
options: Treat and refer urgently under child protection
Treat and advise the family about sharing towels at home
Treat and review at the GP in two weeks
Treat and ask the mother to see her own GP
C.why: A sexually transmitted infection in a young child is highly suggestive of sexual abuse; the explanation is unsuitable. Treat and refer urgently.

whyNot.1: Accepting an implausible explanation fails to protect Lily.
whyNot.2: Delaying referral leaves her at risk.
whyNot.3: This is Lily's safeguarding issue, not one for her mother's GP.

C.q: A nurse notices that Jamal, 8, is persistently dirty and smelly at a 9 am clinic and often hungry. The family has recently become homeless. What is the best approach?
options: Record it as material poverty and take no further action
Discuss with the safeguarding lead and refer to social care
Refer under s47, as these are definite signs of neglect
Ask the school nurse to monitor and report back in six months
C.why: CG89 1.3.3: a child persistently smelly and dirty when seen early in the day should make you suspect neglect, and hunger adds to the concern. CG89 1.3.4 asks you to weigh the constraints of poverty, so a referral lets social care decide whether Family Help support or a fuller response is needed.

whyNot.0: Poverty does not mean his needs can be ignored; CG89 1.3.3 features are present.
whyNot.2: The nurse refers; social care decides whether s47 enquiries are needed, and the features are a reason to suspect, not definite proof.
whyNot.3: Six months is too long to leave a hungry child without support.

reteach.title: Four boxes and the clues
reteach.question: How do I match what I see to a category?

blocks.h: Ask what was done, or not done
blocks.body: Something done to the body: physical. Something done to the mind, again and again: emotional. Anything sexual, contact or not, online or offline: sexual. Something not done, persistently, that the child needs: neglect. Then look at the clue against NICE: shape, site, pattern and the explanation. If the explanation does not fit the injury or the child's development, suspect maltreatment.

blocks.text: Children are victims of domestic abuse in their own right. Poverty is not neglect, but unmet needs still need help.

explain.body: Hitting, shaking, throwing, poisoning, burning, scalding, drowning, suffocating, or fabricating or inducing illness.

test.q: Which fracture finding should make a nurse suspect physical abuse in an infant?
options: A greenstick fracture after a witnessed fall
Rib fractures found on X-ray with no history
A fracture in a child with osteogenesis imperfecta
A clavicle fracture noted after a difficult birth
test.why: CG89 1.1.9: occult fractures such as rib fractures in infants, with no predisposing condition or suitable explanation, should make you suspect maltreatment.

whyNot.0: A witnessed fall is a suitable explanation.
whyNot.3: Birth trauma is a known medical explanation.

explain.body: Persistent emotional maltreatment causing severe and persistent effects: worthless or unloved messages, inappropriate expectations, witnessing ill-treatment, serious bullying.

items.label: types of abuse involve some emotional abuse

test.q: Which behaviour in a 6-year-old may be an alerting feature for emotional abuse?
options: Shyness on the first day in hospital
Crying when a parent leaves the ward
Over-friendliness to unfamiliar staff
Asking many questions about a procedure
test.why: CG89 1.4.2 lists indiscriminate affection-seeking and over-friendliness to strangers, including healthcare professionals.

whyNot.0: Shyness in a new place is expected.
whyNot.1: Distress at separation is a normal attachment response.
whyNot.3: Curiosity about a procedure is healthy.

explain.body: Forcing or enticing a child into sexual activity, contact or non-contact, including grooming, online abuse and coerced self-generated images. Women and children can abuse.

test.q: An adult asks a 12-year-old online to send sexual images of herself. How is this classified?
options: Online bullying
Emotional abuse
Neglect of supervision
Sexual abuse
test.why: Non-contact activity, including coercing a child to produce sexual images, is sexual abuse.

whyNot.1: Emotional harm may result, but the act is sexual abuse.
whyNot.2: Supervision may be relevant, but the act is sexual abuse by the adult.

explain.body: Persistent failure to meet basic physical or psychological needs, likely to seriously impair health or development. Can start in pregnancy through maternal substance use.

test.q: A baby has neonatal abstinence syndrome after his mother used heroin throughout pregnancy and missed antenatal care. Which category does Working Together 2026 use for this?
options: Neglect
Physical abuse
Emotional abuse
Fabricated or induced illness
test.why: Working Together 2026: neglect may occur during pregnancy as a result of maternal substance abuse.

whyNot.1: The guidance classes prenatal substance exposure as neglect.
whyNot.2: Emotional abuse concerns maltreatment of the child's emotional development.
whyNot.3: FII involves fabricating or inducing illness after birth.
